# Setup

```{r packages}
library(tidyverse)   # data manipulation and ggplot2
library(knitr)       # kable() tables
library(patchwork)   # combine plots
library(scales)      # percent labels

theme_set(theme_minimal(base_size = 11))

# Colours used in every chart
status_colours <- c("Employed" = "#2C7FB8", "Unemployed" = "#E6550D")
```

The EDA data is created by `01_Data_Cleaning_EDA_Dashboard.R` and the model data by `02_Data_Preparation_Model.R`.

```{r load-data}
lfs   <- readRDS("../Data/RW_LFS2025_Youth_EDA.rds")    # rich data (EDA)
model <- readRDS("../Data/RW_LFS2025_Youth_Model.rds")  # predictors only (ML)
```

The analysis covers `r format(nrow(lfs), big.mark = ",")` young people
in the labour force. There are `r ncol(model) - 2` candidate predictors.

```{r helpers}
# Small helper functions used in the rest of this document

# Unemployment rate (%) for each category of one variable
unemployment_by <- function(data, variable) {
  data %>%
    group_by(category = .data[[variable]]) %>%
    summarise(
      people     = n(),
      unemployed = sum(employment_status == "Unemployed"),
      rate       = unemployed / people
    )
}

# Bar chart of the unemployment rate by category
plot_rate <- function(data, variable, title) {
  overall <- mean(data$employment_status == "Unemployed")

  unemployment_by(data, variable) %>%
    ggplot(aes(x = rate, y = fct_rev(category))) +
    geom_col(fill = status_colours["Unemployed"], width = 0.7) +
    geom_vline(xintercept = overall, linetype = "dashed") +
    geom_text(aes(label = percent(rate, accuracy = 0.1)),
              hjust = -0.15, size = 3) +
    scale_x_continuous(labels = percent,
                       expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.25))) +
    labs(title = title, x = "Unemployment rate", y = NULL)
}

# Cramer's V: strength of association between two categorical variables
# (0 = no association, 1 = perfect association)
cramers_v <- function(x, y) {
  tab  <- table(x, y)
  chi2 <- suppressWarnings(chisq.test(tab, correct = FALSE)$statistic)
  k    <- min(nrow(tab), ncol(tab)) - 1
  as.numeric(sqrt(chi2 / (sum(tab) * k)))
}
```

# Dataset description

```{r variable-table}
describe_variable <- function(x) {
  if (is.numeric(x)) {
    paste0("Numeric, ", min(x, na.rm = TRUE), " to ", max(x, na.rm = TRUE))
  } else {
    paste0("Categorical, ", nlevels(x), " groups")
  }
}

variable_info <- tibble(
  Variable = names(model)[-(1:2)],
  Type     = map_chr(model[-(1:2)], describe_variable)
)

variable_info %>%
  kable(caption = "Candidate predictors used for machine learning",
        booktabs = TRUE)
```

# Outcome: employment status

```{r outcome, fig.height = 3}
outcome <- lfs %>%
  count(employment_status) %>%
  mutate(share = n / sum(n))

ggplot(outcome, aes(x = employment_status, y = share,
                    fill = employment_status)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.6, show.legend = FALSE) +
  geom_text(aes(label = paste0(percent(share, accuracy = 0.1),
                               "\n(n = ", comma(n), ")")),
            vjust = -0.3, size = 3.5) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = status_colours) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = percent, limits = c(0, 1)) +
  labs(title = "Employment status of youth in the labour force",
       x = NULL, y = "Share of youth")
```

The classes are **imbalanced**. About 1 in 7 young people is unemployed.
A model that predicts "Employed" for everyone would be about 85% accurate
and still useless. Accuracy alone is therefore not a good metric. We will
use recall, F1 and MCC for the unemployed class, and ROC/PR-AUC.

```{r weighted-rate}
weighted_rate <- lfs %>%
  summarise(rate = weighted.mean(employment_status == "Unemployed",
                                 w = survey_weight))
```

The sample rate is `r percent(mean(lfs$employment_status == "Unemployed"), 0.1)`.
Using survey weights, the youth unemployment rate is
`r percent(weighted_rate$rate, 0.1)`.

# Missing values

```{r missing-table}
tvet_vars     <- c("tvet_duration", "tvet_completed", "activity_after_tvet",
                   "time_to_job_after_tvet")
time_use_vars <- c("collects_firewood", "fetches_water", "household_chores",
                   "care_work")
unemp_vars    <- c("unemployment_duration", "ever_worked_before",
                   "main_income_source")
employee_vars <- c("contract_type", "social_security", "paid_leave",
                   "how_job_found", "income_band", "income_cash")

reason_for <- function(v) {
  case_when(
    v %in% tvet_vars     ~ "Asked only to youth with TVET",
    v %in% time_use_vars ~ "Non-response (not filled in)",
    v %in% unemp_vars    ~ "Asked only to unemployed youth",
    v %in% employee_vars ~ "Asked only to paid employees",
    v == "commute_mode"  ~ "Asked only to youth working away from home",
    TRUE                 ~ "Asked only to employed youth"
  )
}

tibble(
  Variable = names(lfs),
  Missing  = colSums(is.na(lfs))
) %>%
  filter(Missing > 0) %>%
  mutate(Percent = percent(Missing / nrow(lfs), accuracy = 0.1),
         Reason  = reason_for(Variable)) %>%
  arrange(desc(Missing)) %>%
  kable(caption = "Variables with missing values (EDA dataset)",
        booktabs = TRUE)
```

Almost all of these are **structural** missing values: the question was not
asked to that person. They are not filled in. Variables asked to only the
employed or only the unemployed are not used as predictors, because they
would give the answer away (data leakage). The only real non-response is in
the time-use questions (about 6%), which are left out of percentages.
The modelling dataset has `r sum(is.na(model))` missing values.

```{r leakage-check}
# Proof of leakage: job sector is missing for every unemployed person
table(Status = lfs$employment_status,
      Sector_missing = is.na(lfs$economic_sector))
```

```{r numeric-summary}
model %>%

  summarise(across(c(age, years_of_schooling, household_size),
                   ~ sprintf("%.1f (%.1f)", mean(.x), sd(.x)))) %>%
  rename(Status = employment_status, Age = age,

```

```{r numeric-plots, fig.height = 3.5}
model %>%
  select(employment_status, age, years_of_schooling, household_size) %>%
  pivot_longer(-employment_status) %>%
  mutate(name = recode(name,
                       age = "Age",
                       years_of_schooling = "Years of schooling",
                       household_size = "Household size")) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = employment_status, y = value, fill = employment_status)) +
  geom_boxplot(show.legend = FALSE, outlier.alpha = 0.3) +
  facet_wrap(~ name, scales = "free_y") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = status_colours) +
  labs(title = "Numeric predictors by employment status", x = NULL, y = NULL)
```

```{r numeric-tests}
# Wilcoxon test: do employed and unemployed youth differ?
numeric_vars <- c("age", "years_of_schooling", "household_size")

map_dfr(numeric_vars, function(v) {
  test <- wilcox.test(model[[v]] ~ model$employment_status)
  tibble(Variable = v, `p-value` = format.pval(test$p.value, digits = 3))
}) %>%
  kable(caption = "Wilcoxon rank-sum tests", booktabs = TRUE)
```

# Feature relevance

## Association with the outcome

We run a chi-square test for each predictor and report Cramér's V, which
measures the strength of the association. Numeric predictors are grouped
into bands first.

```{r association-outcome}
# Put numeric predictors into bands so Cramer's V can be computed
model_banded <- model %>%
  mutate(
    age                = cut(age, c(15, 20, 25, 30)),
    years_of_schooling = cut(years_of_schooling, c(-1, 0, 6, 9, 12, 25)),
    household_size     = cut(household_size, c(0, 2, 4, 6, 10))
  )

predictors <- names(model)[-(1:2)]

relevance <- map_dfr(predictors, function(v) {
  tab <- table(model_banded[[v]], model_banded$employment_status)
  tibble(
    Variable      = v,
    `Chi-square`  = round(chisq.test(tab)$statistic, 1),
    `p-value`     = format.pval(chisq.test(tab)$p.value, digits = 3),
    `Cramer's V`  = round(cramers_v(model_banded[[v]],
                                    model_banded$employment_status), 3)
  )
}) %>%
  arrange(desc(`Cramer's V`))

relevance %>%
  kable(caption = "Association of each predictor with employment status",
        booktabs = TRUE)
```

```{r relevance-plot, fig.height = 4}
ggplot(relevance, aes(x = `Cramer's V`,
                      y = fct_reorder(Variable, `Cramer's V`))) +
  geom_col(fill = status_colours["Employed"], width = 0.7) +
  labs(title = "Strength of association with employment status",
       x = "Cramer's V", y = NULL)
```

## Association between predictors

Predictors that are strongly linked to each other carry the same
information. This matters most for logistic regression.

```{r association-matrix, fig.height = 8, fig.width = 9}
pairs <- expand_grid(var1 = predictors, var2 = predictors)

pairs$v <- map2_dbl(pairs$var1, pairs$var2,
                    ~ cramers_v(model_banded[[.x]], model_banded[[.y]]))

ggplot(pairs, aes(x = var1, y = var2, fill = v)) +
  geom_tile(colour = "white") +
  geom_text(aes(label = sprintf("%.2f", v)), size = 2.5) +
  scale_fill_gradient(low = "white", high = "#2C7FB8", limits = c(0, 1)) +
  labs(title = "Cramer's V between predictors", x = NULL, y = NULL,
       fill = "V") +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1))
```

```{r strong-pairs}
pairs %>%
  filter(var1 < var2, v >= 0.5) %>%
  arrange(desc(v)) %>%
  mutate(v = round(v, 2)) %>%
  rename(`Variable 1` = var1, `Variable 2` = var2, `Cramer's V` = v) %>%
  kable(caption = "Strongly related predictor pairs (V >= 0.5)",
        booktabs = TRUE)
```

# Employed youth: job quality (descriptive only)

These variables only exist for employed youth. They describe the
*quality* of youth jobs and are not used for prediction.

```{r job-quality, fig.height = 7, fig.width = 9}
share_plot <- function(variable, title) {
  lfs %>%
    filter(employment_status == "Employed", !is.na(.data[[variable]])) %>%
    count(category = .data[[variable]]) %>%
    mutate(share = n / sum(n)) %>%
    ggplot(aes(x = share, y = fct_reorder(category, share))) +
    geom_col(fill = status_colours["Employed"], width = 0.7) +
    geom_text(aes(label = percent(share, accuracy = 1)),
              hjust = -0.15, size = 3) +
    scale_x_continuous(labels = percent,
                       expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.2))) +
    labs(title = title, x = "Share of employed youth", y = NULL)
}

share_plot("formal_informal_work", "Formal vs informal work") +
  share_plot("time_underemployment", "Time-related underemployment") +
  share_plot("economic_sector", "Sector of employment") +
  plot_layout(ncol = 1, heights = c(1, 1, 1.5))
```

# Key findings

1. **Imbalanced outcome.** 14.7% of youth in the labour force are
   unemployed. Models must be judged on recall, F1 and MCC for the
   unemployed class, not on accuracy.
2. **Education paradox.** Unemployment rises with education: about 13% for
   youth with no or primary schooling, 22.5% for upper secondary and 17.8%
   for university graduates. Educated youth often wait for a suitable job,
   while less educated youth take any (often informal) work.
3. **Gender gap.** Young women are more often unemployed (17.4%) than young
   men (12.3%).
4. **Household position matters most.** Household heads have the lowest rate
   (8%), while sons, daughters and grandchildren of the head are near 19%.
   Domestic workers are almost never unemployed, because living in as a
   domestic worker already means having a job.
5. **Age.** Unemployment peaks between ages 18 and 23, then falls.
6. **Weak signals.** No single predictor is strongly associated with the
   outcome (all Cramér's V < 0.2). Residence and disability show no
   significant association. Prediction will therefore be modest.
7. **Redundant predictors.** Education level and years of schooling are
   strongly related (V = 0.68), and so are province and residence. Keep only
   one of each pair for logistic regression. Tree-based models can use both.
